title: When Attention Beats Fourier: Multi-Scale Transformers for PDE Solving on Irregular Domains

paper.title: When Attention Beats Fourier: Multi-Scale Transformers for PDE Solving on Irregular Domains
paper.abstract:
Abstract We study the problem of architecture selection for deep learning
models trained to solve partial differential equations (PDEs), asking
when transformer-based architectures with learned attention outperform
Fourier-domain neural operators. We introduce the Multi-Scale
Attention Transformer ( MSAT ), a deep learning architecture that
encodes spatiotemporal solution histories as token sequences and trains
end-to-end via a composite supervised objective with optional
physics-informed regularization terms. We conduct a comprehensive
empirical evaluation against nine baselines—including physics-informed
neural networks (PINNs), neural operators (FNO, DeepONet, GNOT), and
state-space models (Mamba-NO)—across five benchmark problems from the
PINNacle suite, using identical train/test splits and reference data for
all methods. MSAT achieves state-of-the-art generalization on complex
geometry problems ( L rel 2 = 0.0101 L^{2}_{\mathrm{rel}}=0.0101 on Heat2D-CG, a 3.7 × 3.7\times improvement over FNO) at 34 ​ s 34\,\mathrm{s} total inference vs. 120,812 ​ s 120{,}812\,\mathrm{s} for Mamba-NO. Ablation studies over the physics regularization component
reveal a precise inductive bias tradeoff: physics priors reduce test error
on diffusion-dominated problems but degrade generalization on chaotic and
recirculating-flow regimes, directly characterizing the prior misspecification
boundary. Approximation error bounds as a function of domain boundary
complexity κ \kappa provide a theoretical basis for these empirical findings
and a principled rule for architecture selection.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for scientific computing, with neural network architectures trained end-to-end to approximate the solution maps of partial differential equations (PDEs). The central open question in this area is not whether deep learning can solve PDEs—it clearly can—but which architecture and training objective is most appropriate for a given problem class . This paper answers that question empirically and theoretically for the class of complex geometry problems. Two architectural families dominate the literature. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) Raissi et al. (2019) train a network to minimize a composite loss of supervised data fit and PDE residuals at collocation points, exploiting automatic differentiation to enforce governing equations as a regularizer. PINNs generalize well on steady-state problems with well-posed residuals but exhibit poor generalization on chaotic systems, high-frequency solutions, and long rollouts Wang et al. (2021) ; Krishnapriyan et al. (2021) . Neural operators Kovachki et al. (2023) take a function-space learning perspective: they train deep networks to map between spaces of input functions and output functions, enabling zero-shot generalization to new initial conditions. The Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) Li et al. (2021) parametrizes the kernel of the solution operator in frequency space via learned spectral convolutions, achieving strong generalization on smooth periodic benchmarks. However, FNO’s architecture encodes a hard inductive bias: spectral truncation to the lowest K K Fourier modes. On domains with irregular geometry, this truncation systematically discards high-frequency modes excited by boundary effects, limiting generalization. Transformer architectures Vaswani et al. (2017) compute data-dependent, position-wise attention over all input tokens, implementing a learned kernel that adapts to the input distribution without fixed-basis constraints. This makes transformers natural candidates for irregular geometry settings where FNO’s spectral inductive bias is mismatched. We test this hypothesis systematically through a large-scale empirical evaluation, supported by approximation-theoretic analysis. Contributions: 1. MSAT architecture : a multi-scale attention transformer trained with a composite supervised + physics-regularized objective, with optional constraint integration via differentiable loss terms. 2. Benchmark evaluation : nine-model comparison across five PDE benchmarks from PINNacle Hao et al. (2024) , with identical data pipelines, train/test splits, and COMSOL reference ground truth for all baselines. 3. Pareto analysis : joint accuracy-runtime characterization establishing MSAT as the Pareto-dominant deep learning method on geometry-rich problems. 4. Inductive bias characterization : ablation over the physics regularization component precisely identifies the prior misspecification boundary, with supporting approximation error bounds.

sections.heading: Physics-Informed Neural Networks.
sections.text: Raissi et al. Raissi et al. (2019) introduced PINNs as a supervised learning framework that augments the training objective with PDE residual terms evaluated at collocation points via automatic differentiation. Subsequent work addressed training instabilities—including gradient imbalance between loss terms and spectral bias in deep networks—through adaptive loss weighting Wang et al. (2024) (PINN-LRA), residual-adaptive resampling Lu et al. (2021b) (RAR), and domain decomposition Moseley et al. (2023) (FBPINN). Despite these advances, PINNs exhibit poor generalization on chaotic and high-frequency regimes Krishnapriyan et al. (2021) , a phenomenon attributed to the mismatch between the collocation prior and the problem’s frequency content.

sections.heading: Neural Operators and Deep Learning Architectures for PDEs.
sections.text: Neural operators frame PDE solving as a function-space learning problem, training deep networks to generalize across initial conditions. DeepONet Lu et al. (2021a) uses a branch/trunk decomposition inspired by the universal approximation theorem for operators. FNO Li et al. (2021) parametrizes the solution operator in frequency space via learnable spectral convolutions, achieving strong generalization on smooth benchmarks with periodic structure. GNOT Hao et al. (2023) replaces spectral convolutions with cross-attention, extending operator learning to heterogeneous geometries. Mamba-NO applies selective state-space models Gu and Dao (2024) as neural operators, achieving competitive accuracy on structured benchmarks but at impractical cost in the sequential-scan formulation.

sections.heading: Transformers and Attention Mechanisms in Machine Learning.
sections.text: The transformer architecture Vaswani et al. (2017) has become the dominant deep learning paradigm across modalities, with scaled dot-product attention enabling data-dependent, position-wise representation learning that generalizes well across diverse input distributions. Recent work has applied attention to scientific computing Li et al. (2024) ; Cao (2021) , demonstrating that learned kernels can outperform fixed-basis operators on non-periodic domains. Our work provides the first systematic benchmark comparing transformers, spectral operators, SSMs, and PINNs on a diverse PDE suite, with ablations isolating the contribution of physics-informed regularization as a training signal.

sections.heading: Inductive Bias and Architecture Selection in Deep Learning.
sections.text: The question of which neural network architecture best matches a given problem structure is a central theme in machine learning theory mitchell1997machine . Spectral methods encode a periodic inductive bias; convolutional networks encode translation equivariance; attention encodes permutation equivariance with global receptive field. Our work characterizes this question empirically and theoretically for the PDE domain, establishing boundary complexity κ \kappa as the key variable governing architecture selection.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: We frame PDE solving as a supervised sequence regression task, enabling end-to-end training with standard deep learning infrastructure. Given a PDE ℱ ​ [ u ] ​ ( 𝐱 , t ) = 0 \mathcal{F}[u](\mathbf{x},t)=0 on Ω × [ 0 , T ] \Omega\times[0,T] with boundary and initial conditions on ∂ Ω \partial\Omega , we construct a dataset of labeled examples from observed solution snapshots { u ⁡ ( 𝐱 i , t j ) } \{u(\mathbf{x}_{i},t_{j})\} generated by a reference solver. For each spatial point 𝐱 j \mathbf{x}_{j} , the input token sequence is 𝐬 j = [ ( 𝐱 j , t k , u ⁡ ( 𝐱 j , t k ) ) ] k = 1 T in \mathbf{s}_{j}=[(\mathbf{x}_{j},t_{k},u(\mathbf{x}_{j},t_{k}))]_{k=1}^{T_{\mathrm{in}}} and the supervised target is u ⁡ ( 𝐱 j , t ∗ ) u(\mathbf{x}_{j},t^{*}) . The model is trained to minimize a supervised loss over this dataset, with an optional physics-informed regularization term. At test time, the trained model generalizes to unseen query points not in the training split.

sections.heading: 3.3 Physics-Informed Constraints
sections.text: When physics constraints are enabled, MSAT appends a PhysicsInformedLayer that maps the latent representation 𝐳 \mathbf{z} to constraint residuals via sub-networks for PDE-specific physical priors. For the PDE benchmark, we implement three generic constraint types: (i) a mass conservation residual ℒ mass \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mass}} that penalizes divergence of the predicted flux field, (ii) an energy dissipation residual ℒ energy \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{energy}} that penalizes non-monotone energy growth in dissipative systems, and (iii) a spatial smoothness regularizer ℒ smooth \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}} that penalizes large second-order spatial gradients: ℒ phys = λ 1 ​ ℒ mass + λ 2 ​ ℒ energy + λ 3 ​ ℒ smooth , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phys}}=\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mass}}+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{energy}}+\lambda_{3}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}}, where λ i ≥ 0 \lambda_{i}\geq 0 are learnable non-negative scalar weights initialized to 0.1 0.1 . The total training objective is: ℒ = ℒ MSE + ℒ phys , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phys}}, where ℒ MSE = ‖ u ^ − u ‖ 2 2 / ‖ u ‖ 2 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}=\|\hat{u}-u\|_{2}^{2}/\|u\|_{2}^{2} is the normalized mean-squared error on labeled data. In our PDE benchmark, we treat the physics layer as an ablation variable to characterize its domain dependence (Section 4.4 ). Remark 3.2 . The physics constraint terms encode smoothness assumptions that are well-matched to diffusion-dominated and advection-diffusion problems but are misspecified for chaotic systems (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky) and unsteady recirculating flows (NS2D lid-driven cavity). This misspecification is the primary driver of the performance degradation observed in the ablation study.

sections.heading: 3.4 Implementation Details
sections.text: MSAT uses embedding dimension d = 256 d=256 , H = 8 H=8 attention heads, L = 6 L=6 transformer layers, FFN hidden dimension 512, and S = 4 S=4 attention scales. Training uses Adam with initial learning rate η = 10 − 3 \eta=10^{-3} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler (factor 0.5, patience 5), and early stopping (patience 20). All experiments use PINNacle COMSOL reference solutions as ground truth, loaded via the same data pipeline as FNO/GNOT/DeepONet baselines to ensure fair comparison. Batch size 64, bf16 AMP on A100. Full hyperparameter details are given in Appendix A .

sections.text: Table 1 presents the full comparison. We highlight three findings. Finding 1: MSAT is state-of-the-art on complex geometry. On Heat2D-CG—the most geometrically complex benchmark— MSAT achieves L rel 2 = 0.0101 L^{2}_{\mathrm{rel}}=0.0101 , compared to FNO at 0.0379 0.0379 ( 3.7 × 3.7\times worse), Mamba-NO at 0.0209 0.0209 ( 2.1 × 2.1\times worse), and GNOT at 0.117 0.117 ( 11.6 × 11.6\times worse). All PINN variants achieve L rel 2 > 0.025 L^{2}_{\mathrm{rel}}>0.025 despite Heat2D-CG being a diffusion problem naturally suited to PINN collocation. The advantage is attributable to MSAT ’s attention mechanism, which captures long-range spatial dependencies across the irregular domain without the frequency truncation imposed by FNO’s spectral convolution. Finding 2: Spectral methods dominate smooth periodic problems. On Burgers1D, FNO achieves L rel 2 = 0.0034 L^{2}_{\mathrm{rel}}=0.0034 —the best result in the table—while MSAT achieves 0.0156 0.0156 . On KS, Mamba-NO achieves 0.0203 0.0203 and MSAT achieves 0.0357 0.0357 . This is consistent with the theoretical expectation that frequency-domain methods with strong periodic inductive bias outperform general-purpose architectures on problems with smooth, periodic solutions. The steady-state nature of the lid-driven cavity problem—where the PDE residual directly encodes momentum balance—favors collocation-based methods. sections.heading: 4.3 Accuracy-Runtime Pareto Analysis
sections.text: The Pareto plot (omitted for space) plots L rel 2 L^{2}_{\mathrm{rel}} on Heat2D-CG against total compute time. MSAT (no physics) achieves the best accuracy at 34 seconds total inference. FNO achieves 3.7 × 3.7\times worse accuracy at comparable cost (634 s). Mamba-NO achieves 2.1 × 2.1\times worse accuracy at 3,553 × 3{,}553\times higher cost. The Pareto frontier on geometry-rich problems is clearly occupied by MSAT . We note that Mamba-NO’s runtime reflects the pure-PyTorch sequential scan implementation, which scales as 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(N) per layer for sequence length N N without the compiled CUDA kernels required for the fast parallel scan. With compiled kernels, Mamba-NO’s runtime would likely reduce by ∼ 100 × \sim\!100\times ; nonetheless the architectural comparison on accuracy remains valid. FNO’s per-forward-pass complexity is 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) \mathcal{O}(N\log N) due to the FFT, while MSAT ’s attention scales as 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 2 ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(N^{2}d) in the standard formulation; however, because MSAT operates on point-level token sequences of length T in ≪ N grid T_{\mathrm{in}}\ll N_{\mathrm{grid}} , the practical inference cost is substantially lower.

This pattern is interpretable. The physics sub-networks encode mass conservation, energy dissipation, and spatial smoothness priors—constraints well-matched to diffusion and advection-diffusion problems. The Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation involves fourth-order spatial derivatives and chaotic dynamics that violate these smoothness assumptions. Similarly, the unsteady recirculation in NS2D lid-driven cavity is poorly captured by the static gradient priors encoded in the physics layer. This finding is consistent with recent theoretical work showing that physics-informed priors improve generalization when the prior is well-specified but introduce bias-variance tradeoff degradation when the prior is misspecified Wang et al. (2021) . We view this as a positive result: it precisely characterizes the regime boundary of physics-informed priors, enabling practitioners to make principled decisions about when to enable them.

The attention mechanism, by contrast, can allocate tokens to boundary regions without mode truncation, explaining the 3.7 × 3.7\times empirical improvement.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: MSAT is a point-prediction model: it predicts u u at individual spatiotemporal points rather than learning a full solution operator. This means it requires a new forward pass per query point, unlike FNO which predicts the full field in one pass. For applications requiring dense field prediction, neural operators may be preferable despite their accuracy disadvantage on complex geometry. The physics constraints are generic (mass conservation, energy dissipation, spatial smoothness) and are not derived from the specific governing equations of each benchmark PDE. Future work should investigate automatic constraint derivation from symbolic PDE specifications, enabling problem-agnostic physics-informed training. MSAT ’s strong Heat2D-CG performance comes at modestly higher training complexity than FNO; the early stopping mechanism mitigates this in practice but hyperparameter sensitivity warrants further study.

sections.heading: Broader implications.
sections.text: Our results suggest that the field’s current emphasis on spectral neural operators may underserve applications in complex geometry domains, which are common in engineering practice (multi-material composites, fracture mechanics, biological tissue modeling). Attention-based architectures deserve more systematic investigation in these regimes.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We have presented MSAT , a multi-scale attention architecture for PDE solving, and evaluated it comprehensively against the major families of physics-informed ML methods. The central finding is that MSAT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on complex geometry diffusion problems ( 3.7 × 3.7\times improvement over FNO on Heat2D-CG) at negligible inference cost, while competitive methods that achieve comparable accuracy on other benchmarks (Mamba-NO on KS) do so at three orders of magnitude higher compute cost. Ablation studies identify the precise regime where physics-informed priors help: diffusion-dominated problems where the prior’s smoothness assumptions are satisfied. These findings motivate a theory of architecture-problem alignment for neural PDE solvers: spectral methods with periodic inductive bias excel on smooth periodic problems; attention-based methods excel on irregular geometry; collocation-based PINNs excel on steady-state problems with well-posed residuals. Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 formalize this alignment theory through approximation error bounds as a function of domain boundary complexity κ \kappa , providing a principled basis for architecture selection in practice.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2605.08318v1 [cs.LG] 08 May 2026 When Attention Beats Fourier: Multi-Scale Transformers for PDE Solving on Irregular Domains Brandon Yee Email: b.yee@ycrg-labs.org Pairie Koh Affiliation: Physics Lab, Yee Collins Research Group Email: p.koh@ycrg-labs.org Jack Rodriguez Affiliation: Physics Lab, Yee Collins Research Group Email: jasadriguez@gmail.com Mihir Tekal Affiliation: Physics Lab, Yee Collins Research Group Email: m.k.tekal@gmail.com Abstract We study the problem of architecture selection for deep learning models trained to solve partial differential equations (PDEs), asking when transformer-based architectures with learned attention outperform Fourier-domain neural operators. We introduce the Multi-Scale Attention Transformer ( MSAT ), a deep learning architecture that encodes spatiotemporal solution histories as token sequences and trains end-to-end via a composite supervised objective with optional physics-informed regularization terms. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation against nine baselines—including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), neural operators (FNO, DeepONet, GNOT), and state-space models (Mamba-NO)—across five benchmark problems from the PINNacle suite, using identical train/test splits and reference data for all methods. MSAT achieves state-of-the-art generalization on complex geometry problems ( L rel 2 = 0.0101 L^{2}_{\mathrm{rel}}=0.0101 on Heat2D-CG, a 3.7 × 3.7	imes improvement over FNO) at 34 ​ s 34\,\mathrm{s} total inference vs. 120,812 ​ s 120{,}812\,\mathrm{s} for Mamba-NO. Ablation studies over the physics regularization component reveal a precise inductive bias tradeoff: physics priors reduce test error on diffusion-dominated problems but degrade generalization on chaotic and recirculating-flow regimes, directly characterizing the prior misspecification boundary. Approximation error bounds as a function of domain boundary complexity κ \kappa provide a theoretical basis for these empirical findings and a principled rule for architecture selection. 1 Introduction Deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for scientific computing, with neural network architectures trained end-to-end to approximate the solution maps of partial differential equations (PDEs). The central open question in this area is not whether deep learning can solve PDEs—it clearly can—but which architecture and training objective is most appropriate for a given problem class . This paper answers that question empirically and theoretically for the class of complex geometry problems. Two architectural families dominate the literature. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) Raissi et al. (2019) train a network to minimize a composite loss of supervised data fit and PDE residuals at collocation points, exploiting automatic differentiation to enforce governing equations as a regularizer. PINNs generalize well on steady-state problems with well-posed residuals but exhibit poor generalization on chaotic systems, high-frequency solutions, and long rollouts Wang et al. (2021) ; Krishnapriyan et al. (2021) . Neural operators Kovachki et al. (2023) take a function-space learning perspective: they train deep networks to map between spaces of input functions and output functions, enabling zero-shot generalization to new initial conditions. The Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) Li et al. (2021) parametrizes the kernel of the solution operator in frequency space via learned spectral convolutions, achieving strong generalization on smooth periodic benchmarks. However, FNO’s architecture encodes a hard inductive bias: spectral truncation to the lowest K K Fourier modes. On domains with irregular geometry, this truncation systematically discards high-frequency modes excited by boundary effects, limiting generalization. Transformer architectures Vaswani et al. (2017) compute data-dependent, position-wise attention over all input tokens, implementing a learned kernel that adapts to the input distribution without fixed-basis constraints. This makes transformers natural candidates for irregular geometry settings where FNO’s spectral inductive bias is mismatched. We test this hypothesis systematically through a large-scale empirical evaluation, supported by approximation-theoretic analysis. Contributions: 1. MSAT architecture : a multi-scale attention transformer trained with a composite supervised + physics-regularized objective, with optional constraint integration via differentiable loss terms. 2. Benchmark evaluation : nine-model comparison across five PDE benchmarks from PINNacle Hao et al. (2024) , with identical data pipelines, train/test splits, and COMSOL reference ground truth for all baselines. 3. Pareto analysis : joint accuracy-runtime characterization establishing MSAT as the Pareto-dominant deep learning method on geometry-rich problems. 4. Inductive bias characterization : ablation over the physics regularization component precisely identifies the prior misspecification boundary, with supporting approximation error bounds. 2 Related Work Physics-Informed Neural Networks. Raissi et al. Raissi et al. (2019) introduced PINNs as a supervised learning framework that augments the training objective with PDE residual terms evaluated at collocation points via automatic differentiation. Subsequent work addressed training instabilities—including gradient imbalance between loss terms and spectral bias in deep networks—through adaptive loss weighting Wang et al. (2024) (PINN-LRA), residual-adaptive resampling Lu et al. (2021b) (RAR), and domain decomposition Moseley et al. (2023) (FBPINN). Despite these advances, PINNs exhibit poor generalization on chaotic and high-frequency regimes Krishnapriyan et al. (2021) , a phenomenon attributed to the mismatch between the collocation prior and the problem’s frequency content. Neural Operators and Deep Learning Architectures for PDEs. Neural operators frame PDE solving as a function-space learning problem, training deep networks to generalize across initial conditions. DeepONet Lu et al. (2021a) uses a branch/trunk decomposition inspired by the universal approximation theorem for operators. FNO Li et al. (2021) parametrizes the solution operator in frequency space via learnable spectral convolutions, achieving strong generalization on smooth benchmarks with periodic structure. GNOT Hao et al. (2023) replaces spectral convolutions with cross-attention, extending operator learning to heterogeneous geometries. Mamba-NO applies selective state-space models Gu and Dao (2024) as neural operators, achieving competitive accuracy on structured benchmarks but at impractical cost in the sequential-scan formulation. Transformers and Attention Mechanisms in Machine Learning. The transformer architecture Vaswani et al. (2017) has become the dominant deep learning paradigm across modalities, with scaled dot-product attention enabling data-dependent, position-wise representation learning that generalizes well across diverse input distributions. Recent work has applied attention to scientific computing Li et al. (2024) ; Cao (2021) , demonstrating that learned kernels can outperform fixed-basis operators on non-periodic domains. Our work provides the first systematic benchmark comparing transformers, spectral operators, SSMs, and PINNs on a diverse PDE suite, with ablations isolating the contribution of physics-informed regularization as a training signal. Inductive Bias and Architecture Selection in Deep Learning. The question of which neural network architecture best matches a given problem structure is a central theme in machine learning theory mitchell1997machine . Spectral methods encode a periodic inductive bias; convolutional networks encode translation equivariance; attention encodes permutation equivariance with global receptive field. Our work characterizes this question empirically and theoretically for the PDE domain, establishing boundary complexity κ \kappa as the key variable governing architecture selection. 3 The MSAT Architecture 3.1 Problem Formulation We frame PDE solving as a supervised sequence regression task, enabling end-to-end training with standard deep learning infrastructure. MSAT is a point-prediction model: it predicts u u at individual spatiotemporal points rather than learning a full solution operator. This means it requires a new forward pass per query point, unlike FNO which predicts the full field in one pass. For applications requiring dense field prediction, neural operators may be preferable despite their accuracy disadvantage on complex geometry. The physics constraints are generic (mass conservation, energy dissipation, spatial smoothness) and are not derived from the specific governing equations of each benchmark PDE. Future work should investigate automatic constraint derivation from symbolic PDE specifications, enabling problem-agnostic physics-informed training. MSAT ’s strong Heat2D-CG performance comes at modestly higher training complexity than FNO; the early stopping mechanism mitigates this in practice but hyperparameter sensitivity warrants further study. Broader implications. Our results suggest that the field’s current emphasis on spectral neural operators may underserve applications in complex geometry domains, which are common in engineering practice (multi-material composites, fracture mechanics, biological tissue modeling). Attention-based architectures deserve more systematic investigation in these regimes. 6 Conclusion We have presented MSAT , a multi-scale attention architecture for PDE solving, and evaluated it comprehensively against the major families of physics-informed ML methods. The central finding is that MSAT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on complex geometry diffusion problems ( 3.7 × 3.7	imes improvement over FNO on Heat2D-CG) at negligible inference cost, while competitive methods that achieve comparable accuracy on other benchmarks (Mamba-NO on KS) do so at three orders of magnitude higher compute cost. Ablation studies identify the precise regime where physics-informed priors help: diffusion-dominated problems where the prior’s smoothness assumptions are satisfied. These findings motivate a theory of architecture-problem alignment for neural PDE solvers: spectral methods with periodic inductive bias excel on smooth periodic problems; attention-based methods excel on irregular geometry; collocation-based PINNs excel on steady-state problems with well-posed residuals. Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 formalize this alignment theory through approximation error bounds as a function of domain boundary complexity κ \kappa , providing a principled basis for architecture selection in practice.
